newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Sunni-Shi'ite killings raise tension in Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Sunni-Shi'ite killings raise tension in Pakistan.

text.p: A deadly feud between militants of rival Islamic sects in Pakistan has grown into Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's first major security challenge.
About 70 people have died this year in tit-for-tat attacks by Sunni and Shi'ite zealots and shootings have multiplied ahead of the Shi'ite mourning month of Muharram starting next Friday.
"Every possible measure will be taken to ensure the peaceful passage of the month of Muharram," The News newspaper on Sunday quoted interior minister Shujaat Hussain as saying.
The vendetta has been fought mainly in Lahore and elsewhere in Punjab province, where members of Pakistan's estimated 15 percent Shi'ite minority mingle with majority Sunnis.

Many people see the bloodletting as part of a regional proxy war pitting the clients of Shi'ite Iran against its Arab rivals such as Saudi Arabia and Iraq -- though the protagonists deny receiving any outside support and hard evidence is lacking.
Some Shi'ite leaders voice suspicions that the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency foments trouble for Pakistani Shi'ites to keep them off balance and contain Iranian influence.
Sharif's government, which took power after February 3 elections, is now grappling with a virulent legacy of sectarian unrest which the prime minister has sworn to combat.

In the lower Punjab city of Multan, armed police searched worshippers entering mosques for Friday prayers and enforced a provincial ban on motorcycle pillion-riding to deter hit-and-run attacks by gunmen using grenades and Kalashnikov rifles.
Citizens and officials blame small, hate-filled bands of youthful Sunni and Shi'ite militants for injecting tension into a generally harmonious communal relationship.

"There is an element of fear, but primarily people are living peacefully," Multan's senior superintendent of police Arif Ikram told Reuters. "This sectarian violence is really disturbing the peace and giving the country a bad name."

He said his men were giving special protection to 51 people known to be on the hit-lists of rival groups. Police backed by army units were preparing to guard hundreds of processions and gatherings planned by Shi'ites in the first 10 days of Muharram.

Lashkar-i-Jhangvi, a militant Sunni group, has vowed to stop Shi'ites, whom it regards as heretics, from staging marches that climax in passionate chanting and self-flagellation on the day of Ashura, marking the death of Hussain, the Prophet Mohammed's grandson and Shi'ite hero, in the battle of Karbala in AD 680.
Lashkar-i-Jhangvi is an off-shoot of Sipah-i-Sahaba Pakistan (SSP), founded in the early 1980s to counter newly assertive Shi'ite groups inspired by the 1979 Iranian revolution.
An SSP leader blamed Lashkar-i-Jhangvi for a well-planned attack on the Iranian cultural centre in Multan on February 20 in which eight people, including its Iranian director, died.
Maulana Abdul Qavi said the assault was a reprisal for last September's dawn massacre at the city's Jamia-al-Khair mosque in which more than 20 Sunni worshippers were killed.
He said that attack was the work of Sipah-i-Mohammad Pakistan (SMP), a radical splinter group from the mainstream Shi'ite Tehrik-i-Jafria Pakistan (TJP) movement.

"Islam is a religion of peace...so the SSP and TJP are trying their best to stop this inhuman killing," he said. "But the youths don't want to listen to the leaders of the two sects and have become so extremist it is impossible to stop them."
The SSP's leader, Maulana Zia-ur-Rahman Faruqi, was among 26 people killed in a January 18 bomb blast outside a Lahore courthouse where he had been brought to face murder charges.
Qavi called for renewed efforts by the Milli Yakjehti Council (MYC), grouping several Sunni and Shi'ite religious parties, to quell the violence and foster tolerance.
His appeal was echoed by a prominent Shi'ite, Syed Mazhar Gilani, a member of the TJP's central executive council. "It is necessary to reunite and strengthen the MYC," he said.

But police say the rival groups are well-armed and generously-funded. Some are believed to use neighbouring Afghanistan as a training ground for guerrillas ostensibly destined for the fight against Indian rule in Kashmir.

Since the days of former prime minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto in the 1970s and the military regime of General Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq that followed, Pakistani leaders have often sought to do deals with religious parties for short-term political gain.
Pakistani critics say this political cover has allowed the extremists to flourish. It may now take more than exhortations by religious and government leaders to rein them in.
